Letter to the Editor : serum aminotransferase activity beyond 100
times the upper limit of normal value doesn't suggest acute fatty
liver of pregnancy alone
We read the case report of acute fatty liver of pregnancy
(AFLP) by Wong et al. with interest (1). This report includes two
unusual features. First the onset of illness was early, 18 weeks'
gestation, which was only reported once (2) in 600 cases of
AFLP reported in 25 publications (1998-2020) that we evaluated.
Second, the peak serum alanine aminotransferase (sALAT)
activity was >100 times the upper limit of normal value (ULNV)
on the day of delivery, a value which has only been reported in
one Australian case quoted by Wong (1, reference 5) and in two
US patients. One of the latter patients, who had recently ingested
acetaminophen (ACT), had ACT levels within the therapeutic
range at admission (like Wong's patient), but required liver
transplantation and had liver histology showing microvesicular
steatosis (MS) and centrilobular necrosis confirming ACT
hepatotoxicity (3). It should be noted that in a US study in 70
pregnant women with encephalopathy, the maximum sALAT

activity on admission was 154 IU/L in 14 with AFLP, which was
significantly lower than the mean sALAT value, 2333 IU/L, in 21
others with ACT overdose (4).
Because of the two unusual features in the patient in Wong's
report, the diagnosis of liver lesions should have been clearly
confirmed. However, the diagnosis of AFLP was only determined
by routine liver histology one week after delivery. Figure 1
includes images of MS, but not the entire liver lobule or the
central position of the nucleus in steatotic hepatocytes, an
important feature of MS (1). Thus, the sixth Swansea criteria for
AFLP in this report was not supported by fat-stain on frozen liver
tissue samples for a diagnosis of MS, or liver fat quantification
by repeated magnetic resonance imaging, to diagnose transient
liver
-2-
steatosis during recovery from AFLP (5).
In conclusion, we find it difficult to accept the diagnosis of
isolated AFLP in a patient with sALAT activity >100 times the
ULNV. Moreover, a recent detailed history of the ingestion of

liver disease.
